items.stem: Define the term 'occupier'.
items.answer: A person who has a sufficient degree of control over premises to be under a duty to those who come onto them; there can be more than one occupier (Wheat v E Lacon & Co).

items.stem: Lucas Ltd owns a shopping centre in Bangkok. Grace, an electrician called in to fix a faulty switchboard, received an electric shock from it while working. State, with a brief reason, the most likely legal outcome.
items.answer: Lucas Ltd owed Grace the common duty of care; on these facts it is probably not liable, as the shock was a risk ordinarily incident to an electrician's calling (Roles v Nathan). Reason: s2(2) OLA 1957: the occupier must take reasonable care to see that the visitor is reasonably safe

items.stem: Daniel Ltd owns a shopping centre in Bangkok. Lina, an electrician called in to fix a faulty switchboard, received an electric shock from it while working. Advise Lina whether Daniel Ltd is liable under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957.
items.answer: Law: s2(2) OLA 1957: the occupier must take reasonable care to see that the visitor is reasonably safe; Daniel Ltd is the occupier as it controls the premises (Wheat v Lacon); s2(3)(a) children; s2(3)(b) specialists (Roles v Nathan); s2(4)(a) warnings; s2(4)(b) independent contractors (Haseldine v Daw). Application: Lina is a lawful visitor: a specialist who can be expected to guard against risks of the trade (s2(3)(b); Roles v Nathan); on the facts Daniel Ltd is probably not liable, as the shock was a risk ordinarily incident to an electrician's calling (Roles v Nathan). Conclusion: Daniel Ltd owed Lina the common duty of care; on these facts it is probably not liable, as the shock was a risk ordinarily incident to an electrician's calling (Roles v Nathan).

items.stem: Explain how the common duty of care applies to children and to specialists.
items.answer: Children: the occupier must be prepared for children to be less careful (s2(3)(a)), including allurements (Glasgow Corp v Taylor), though parents are expected to supervise young children (Phipps). Specialists: occupiers can expect them to guard against risks of their trade (s2(3)(b); Roles v Nathan).

items.stem: Explain when an occupier is not liable for the work of an independent contractor.
items.answer: Under s2(4)(b) where the occupier acted reasonably in entrusting the work, took reasonable steps to check the contractor was competent, and checked the work was properly done where possible (Haseldine v Daw); simple tasks may be checked by the occupier (Woodward v Mayor of Hastings).

items.stem: Priya Ltd owns a disused factory on the edge of Toronto. There has never been any sign of anyone entering the site. Lina, aged 25, climbed through a gap in the fence at night and was injured when a rotten floor gave way. Identify the main legal issue raised and state the relevant legal rule.
items.answer: The duty owed to trespassers under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984. S1(3): duty arises if occupier is aware of the danger, knows or believes trespassers may be in the vicinity and the risk is one against which protection is reasonably expected.

items.stem: Amara Ltd owns a disused factory on the edge of Lagos. Local children often play there and Amara Ltd has been told about broken fencing. Diego, aged 9, climbed through a gap in the fence at night and was injured when a rotten floor gave way. Advise Diego whether Amara Ltd is liable under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984. Explain the relevant legal rules before applying them.
items.answer: Law: s1(3): duty arises if occupier is aware of the danger, knows or believes trespassers may be in the vicinity and the risk is one against which protection is reasonably expected; s1(4): reasonable care to see the trespasser is not injured; s1(5) warnings; s1(6) willing acceptance of risk (Ratcliff); obvious risks from own activity (Tomlinson; Keown); only personal injury is covered (s1(8)). Application: knowledge of likely trespassers, so a duty may arise; the injury arose from a danger due to the state of the premises; Diego's age (9) is relevant to whether the danger was obvious. Conclusion: Liability depends on whether s1(3) is satisfied: here there is knowledge of likely trespassers, so a duty may arise and the injury came from a danger due to the state of the premises.

items.stem: Lucas lives in a busy industrial district of Santiago. Priya opened a late-night bar next door with loud music until 3 am every night. Lucas complains of lack of sleep and stress. Advise Lucas whether Priya has committed a private nuisance and what remedies are available. Explain the relevant legal rules before applying them.
items.answer: Law: private nuisance is an unreasonable interference with the use or enjoyment of land; the claimant needs a proprietary interest (Hunter v Canary Wharf); factors: locality (Sturges v Bridgman), duration (Crown River Cruises), sensitivity (Robinson v Kilvert), malice (Christie v Davey); coming to the nuisance is no defence (Coventry v Lawrence); remedies: injunction, possibly limited (Kennaway v Thompson), or damages in lieu. Application: Lucas must have a proprietary interest to sue; the area is an industrial area where some noise and smell are expected (Sturges v Bridgman); Priya's activity is continuous, so more likely to be unreasonable. Conclusion: Priya's conduct is likely to be a nuisance if, weighing these factors, it is unreasonable; Lucas may seek an injunction or damages.

items.answer: For: provides a basic level of protection, especially for children; reasonable balance with occupiers' rights; warnings and fencing can discharge the duty. Conclusion: The Act gives limited but reasonable protection, rightly focused on dangers from the state of the premises.

items.stem: Define the term 'locality'.
items.answer: The character of the neighbourhood, which affects whether an interference with comfort is unreasonable (Sturges v Bridgman).

items.stem: Using Robinson v Kilvert (1889) as an example, explain how the courts approach private nuisance.
items.answer: Facts: heat from a cellar damaged sensitive brown paper stored above it. Principle: There is no liability for harm caused only because the claimant's use is abnormally sensitive. This shows how the law on private nuisance is applied.

items.stem: Yusuf lives in a busy industrial district of Lima. Mohammed opened a late-night bar next door with loud music until 3 am every night. Yusuf complains of lack of sleep and stress. State, with a brief reason, the most likely legal outcome.
items.answer: Mohammed's conduct is likely to be a nuisance if, weighing these factors, it is unreasonable; Yusuf may seek an injunction or damages. Reason: private nuisance is an unreasonable interference with the use or enjoyment of land; the claimant needs a proprietary interest (Hunter v Canary Wharf)

items.stem: Omar lives in a busy industrial district of Kathmandu. Sipho opened a late-night bar next door with loud music until 3 am every night. Omar complains of lack of sleep and stress. Advise Omar whether Sipho has committed a private nuisance and what remedies are available. Refer to at least one decided case.
items.answer: Law: private nuisance is an unreasonable interference with the use or enjoyment of land; the claimant needs a proprietary interest (Hunter v Canary Wharf); factors: locality (Sturges v Bridgman), duration (Crown River Cruises), sensitivity (Robinson v Kilvert), malice (Christie v Davey); coming to the nuisance is no defence (Coventry v Lawrence); remedies: injunction, possibly limited (Kennaway v Thompson), or damages in lieu. Application: Omar must have a proprietary interest to sue; the area is an industrial area where some noise and smell are expected (Sturges v Bridgman); Sipho's activity is continuous, so more likely to be unreasonable. Conclusion: Sipho's conduct is likely to be a nuisance if, weighing these factors, it is unreasonable; Omar may seek an injunction or damages.

items.stem: Evaluate the extent to which private nuisance balances the interests of neighbours.
items.answer: For: flexible reasonable-user test; factors such as locality and malice reflect fairness; Coventry v Lawrence allows damages to protect useful activities. Against: proprietary interest requirement excludes family members (Hunter); outcomes are unpredictable; damages in lieu may let wealthy defendants "buy" the right to cause a nuisance. Conclusion: The tort balances interests reasonably, though access to it is limited.

items.stem: Briefly explain the legal principle established in Read v J Lyons & Co Ltd (1947).
items.answer: Facts: an inspector was injured by an explosion inside a munitions factory. Principle: There must be an escape from the defendant's land.

items.stem: Explain three defences to a claim under Rylands v Fletcher.
items.answer: Act of a stranger (Perry v Kendricks); act of God (Nichols v Marsland); consent of the claimant; statutory authority; default of the claimant.

items.stem: Ravi Ltd stores toxic waste in large tanks on its land in Bangkok. A tank failed because of an unexpected fault. The toxic waste escaped onto Mohammed's neighbouring farm, damaging crops and buildings. Identify the main legal issue raised and state the relevant legal rule.
items.answer: The rule in Rylands v Fletcher. Bringing onto land and accumulating something likely to do mischief if it escapes (Rylands v Fletcher).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the rule in Rylands v Fletcher. 1 mark: states the rule correctly, e.g. bringing onto land and accumulating something likely to do mischief if it escapes (Rylands v Fletcher). [2]

items.stem: Mohammed Ltd stores toxic waste in large tanks on its land in Jakarta. An intruder deliberately opened a valve at night. The toxic waste escaped onto Aisha's neighbouring farm, damaging crops and buildings. (a) Identify the main legal issue raised by these facts. (b) Outline the law that applies, with supporting authority.
items.answer: (a) The rule in Rylands v Fletcher. (b) bringing onto land and accumulating something likely to do mischief if it escapes (Rylands v Fletcher); non-natural use creating an exceptionally high risk (Transco); escape (Read v Lyons) and foreseeable type of damage (Cambridge Water); defences: act of stranger, act of God, consent, statutory authority.
